ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Instituto de Investigaciones Médicas Alfredo Lanari.
-Ethics approval (include appropriate approvals or waivers): This study was approved by the Research Ethics Board at Instituto de Investigaciones Médicas Alfredo Lanari (protocol 355).
During the learning phase, the participants enrolled in a Duolingo Guarani course.

Participants were native speakers of Rioplatense Spanish, a variety spoken mainly in Argentina and Uruguay and characterized by features such as voseo (the use of vos as the second-person singular pronoun) and yeísmo rehilado (the postalveolar fricative realization of /ʝ/ and /ʎ/) (Coloma, 2018; Lipski, 2012; Resnick, 2012).
table.formatted: Participants were native speakers of Rioplatense Spanish, a variety spoken mainly in Argentina and Uruguay and characterized by features such as voseo (the use of vos as the second-person singular pronoun) and yeísmo rehilado (the postalveolar fricative realization of /ʝ/ and /ʎ/) <ref type="bibr">(Coloma, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lipski, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Resnick, 2012)</ref>.

table.text: Participants were 18-35 years old, had no prior knowledge of Guarani (apart from common loanwords in Rioplatense Spanish, such as "chipa" or "tereré", which were not used in the study), and were either undergraduate students or university graduates.
Twenty-four participants (19-35 years; M = 24.75, SD = 4.17; 15 female) completed the required learning assignments and participated in the EEG session.
No participants were excluded due to insufficient learning performance, as all participants who completed the learning phase achieved the predefined learning criteria.

Data from three participants were subsequently excluded from the EEG analyses because of excessive trial rejection or a high proportion of noisy or unusable channels during preprocessing, resulting in a final EEG sample of 21 participants.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.

The standard sequence of lessons provided by Duolingo was not modified for the purposes of this study: participants completed the lessons in the same order and format as regular learners using the platform.
Participants completed 69 lessons, each consisting of 15 tasks.

All participants were exposed to the same set of 155 Guarani (L2) words-including pronouns, nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, conjunctions and interjections-as the course followed a fixed progression.
table.header: Tasks involved bidirectional translations between Spanish (L1) and Guarani (L2).

table.text: Guarani (L2) words were drawn from the first three sections of the Duolingo Guarani course to ensure that all participants had encountered and learned them prior to the EEG session.
Participants were allowed to respond as soon as the target word appeared, and no feedback was provided. answer during the last two screens (in red).
Participants were included only if their overall accuracy exceeded chance level, defined as 50% given the binary nature of the task.
At the behavioral level, participants were more accurate and responded faster to L1 than to L2 targets.

These differences are consistent with the greater familiarity and more extensive experience participants had with L1 vocabulary and provide a broad behavioral indication that L2 processing remained distinct from that of established lexical representations.

Because participants were required to judge whether word pairs were semantically related, the observed effects may involve controlled retrieval and strategic processing, making it difficult to establish the extent to which they reflect automatic semantic activation.
-Consent to participate: Each participant provided informed consent before participation.
Participants were instructed to complete two lessons per day until reaching and completing Section 3.4 of the Duolingo Guarani course.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2007) to estimate the minimum sample size required for an analysis with within-subjects factors. Using α = .05, desired power of 1 -β = .95, and an effect size estimate of f = 0.3, derived from a conservative approach of prior ERP research (Liu & van Hell, 2020), the analysis indicated a minimum sample size of N ≥ 20.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8' to check the contents of 2 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. All essential information could be detected. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "apriori", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = 20, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.95, effect_size = 0.3, effect_size_metric = "Cohen's f", software = "G*Power"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2007) to estimate the minimum sample size required for an analysis with within-subjects factors. Using α = .05, desired power of 1 -β = .95, and an effect size estimate of f = 0.3, derived from a conservative approach of prior ERP research (Liu & van Hell, 2020), the analysis indicated a minimum sample size of N ≥ 20."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 5666 columns across 605 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2332 file/column combinations have at least one issue.
#### Spreadsheet Formatting
We examined 26 spreadsheet files in the repository; 24 have at least one formatting issue.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 605 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

findings.detail: Column name has characters not allowed in file names (":"). Such names break when reused as file names or in code; prefer short names of letters, digits and underscores. A name like this can also mean the file's header was not parsed as intended.

Participants were native speakers of Rioplatense Spanish, a variety spoken mainly in Argentina and Uruguay and characterized by features such as voseo (the use of vos as the second-person singular pronoun) and yeísmo rehilado (the postalveolar fricative realization of /ʝ/ and /ʎ/) (Coloma, 2018; Lipski, 2012; Resnick, 2012).

Participants were 18-35 years old, had no prior knowledge of Guarani (apart from common loanwords in Rioplatense Spanish, such as "chipa" or "tereré", which were not used in the study), and were either undergraduate students or university graduates.
Twenty-four participants (19-35 years; M = 24.75, SD = 4.17; 15 female) completed the required learning assignments and participated in the EEG session.
No participants were excluded due to insufficient learning performance, as all participants who completed the learning phase achieved the predefined learning criteria.

Data from three participants were subsequently excluded from the EEG analyses because of excessive trial rejection or a high proportion of noisy or unusable channels during preprocessing, resulting in a final EEG sample of 21 participants.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.

The standard sequence of lessons provided by Duolingo was not modified for the purposes of this study: participants completed the lessons in the same order and format as regular learners using the platform.
Participants completed 69 lessons, each consisting of 15 tasks.

All participants were exposed to the same set of 155 Guarani (L2) words-including pronouns, nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, conjunctions and interjections-as the course followed a fixed progression.
Guarani (L2) words were drawn from the first three sections of the Duolingo Guarani course to ensure that all participants had encountered and learned them prior to the EEG session.
Participants were allowed to respond as soon as the target word appeared, and no feedback was provided. answer during the last two screens (in red).
Participants were included only if their overall accuracy exceeded chance level, defined as 50% given the binary nature of the task.
At the behavioral level, participants were more accurate and responded faster to L1 than to L2 targets.

These differences are consistent with the greater familiarity and more extensive experience participants had with L1 vocabulary and provide a broad behavioral indication that L2 processing remained distinct from that of established lexical representations.

Because participants were required to judge whether word pairs were semantically related, the observed effects may involve controlled retrieval and strategic processing, making it difficult to establish the extent to which they reflect automatic semantic activation.
-Consent to participate: Each participant provided informed consent before participation.
Participants were instructed to complete two lessons per day until reaching and completing Section 3.4 of the Duolingo Guarani course.

text.text: The consolidation of newly learned vocabulary into semantic memory networks is a critical process in word learning, including second-language (L2) acquisition.

However, most neurocognitive studies of lexical-semantic integration rely on short, artificial learning paradigms, leaving open the question of whether naturalistic, app-based learning produces comparable neural outcomes.

In this study, we combined an ecological learning environment with controlled electrophysiological testing to examine whether vocabulary learned through Duolingo shows neural signatures of semantic integration.

Native Spanish speakers studied Guarani vocabulary for approximately five weeks and subsequently completed a semantic relatedness judgement task during EEG recording that included both L1 (Spanish) and L2 (Guarani) word pairs.

Critically, L2 targets were classified as Remote (trained for an average of 26 days and last practiced 20 days before testing) or Recent (trained for an average of 10 days and last practiced 10 days before testing), allowing us to assess differences associated with learning recency.
Results show that participants responded more accurately and faster to L1 than L2 words.
Although Remote and Recent L2 words did not differ in overall accuracy, response times, or ERP amplitudes, learning recency modulated semantic relatedness effects.
Behaviorally, the accuracy difference between Unrelated and Related trials was smaller for Remote than Recent words.

At Pz, the difference between Unrelated and Related trials in the N400 time window was larger for Remote than Recent words, whereas no corresponding recency-related modulation was observed in the LPC time window.

Together, these findings indicate that newly acquired L2 words can engage semantic processing and that some semantic relatedness effects vary with their learning history, potentially reflecting differences in the recency, amount, and duration of exposure.

More broadly, they demonstrate that naturalistic, app-based language learning can be combined with controlled electrophysiological measures to investigate the neurocognitive processing of newly acquired vocabulary.
Vocabulary acquisition-whether in a first (L1) or second language (L2)-extends beyond the initial mapping between a word's form and its meaning.

Successful word learning involves acquiring phonological and orthographic form, semantic content, as well as ensuring that these representations become stable over time and interact with existing lexical knowledge (e.g., Lindsay & Gaskell, 2010; Lei et al., 2022; Laurino et al., 2022; Rodríguez-Fornells et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Successful word learning involves acquiring phonological and orthographic form, semantic content, as well as ensuring that these representations become stable over time and interact with existing lexical knowledge (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Lindsay & Gaskell, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lei et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Laurino et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rodríguez-Fornells et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Two key processes are typically distinguished in this progression: consolidation, referring to the stabilization and strengthening of newly encoded memory representations (e.g. Dudai et al., 2015; Squire, 2004), and integration, referring to the subsequent embedding of these representations within existing lexical-semantic networks allowing them to interact with other words (e.g., Leach & Samuel, 2007; Tamminen & Gaskell, 2013).

text.text: One influential account of this transition is the Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) framework (McClelland et al., 1995) as applied to word learning (Davis & Gaskell, 2009), which proposes a division of labor between hippocampal and neocortical systems.
text.formatted: One influential account of this transition is the Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) framework <ref type="bibr">(McClelland et al., 1995)</ref> as applied to word learning <ref type="bibr">(Davis & Gaskell, 2009)</ref>, which proposes a division of labor between hippocampal and neocortical systems.

text.text: Within this framework, newly acquired lexical items are initially supported by rapid hippocampal encoding, enabling the formation of sparse, episodic representations that allow for immediate retrieval.
Over time, these representations are gradually reorganized and integrated into distributed neocortical networks, supporting their incorporation into semantic networks.

While this framework has been highly influential, the notion of integration itself requires further clarification, both in terms of behavioral evidence and neural markers, given the heterogeneity of existing findings.
The consolidation-integration distinction is particularly relevant for L2 vocabulary learning, where new lexical forms are acquired within an already established linguistic system.
In this context, the present study examines L2 (Guarani) word learning in a naturalistic environment using the Duolingo language learning app.
Specifically, we investigate whether newly learned L2 words show signatures of lexical-semantic integration by combining behavioral and electroencephalographic (EEG) measures.

By examining lexical integration in a naturalistic learning environment and in a language other than English, this study aims to extend the characterization of how newly acquired L2 words are processed within semantic networks and whether this processing varies as a function of learning recency.

To contextualize these questions, we first review behavioral and electrophysiological evidence of lexical-semantic processing following word learning, before considering the challenges of studying these processes in naturalistic L2 learning environments and in underrepresented languages.
Behavioral studies have examined whether newly learned words show evidence of lexical-semantic links with existing words.
Much of this evidence comes from experimental novel-word learning paradigms in L1, rather than from naturalistic L2 vocabulary learning.
For example, a newly learned word may be recognized more easily when preceded by a familiar related word.
Evidence for these interactions comes from semantic priming tasks, in which a target word is preceded by a semantically related or unrelated prime (e.g., Meyer & Schvaneveldt, 1971; Neely, 1976).
text.formatted: Evidence for these interactions comes from semantic priming tasks, in which a target word is preceded by a semantically related or unrelated prime (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Meyer & Schvaneveldt, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Neely, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: Newly learned words can also influence the processing of related words during lexical selection, leading to slower responses when a related word is presented concurrently with a picture.
This type of competition is typically assessed using picture-word interference tasks (Clay et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This type of competition is typically assessed using picture-word interference tasks <ref type="bibr">(Clay et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, the time course of these effects remains debated.

Delayed effects of lexical interactions have been reported using both semantic priming and picture-word interference paradigms, emerging between approximately 24 hours and seven days after learning (e.g., Dumay & Gaskell, 2007; Tamminen & Gaskell, 2008; Breitenstein et al., 2007; Lei et al., 2022), whereas other studies have reported reliable measures of lexical interactions shortly after learning (e.g., Armstrong et al., 2024; Batterink & Neville, 2011; Coutanche & Thompson-Schill, 2014; Borovsky et al., 2012; Kapnoula & McMurray, 2016).
text.formatted: Delayed effects of lexical interactions have been reported using both semantic priming and picture-word interference paradigms, emerging between approximately 24 hours and seven days after learning (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Dumay & Gaskell, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tamminen & Gaskell, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Breitenstein et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lei et al., 2022)</ref>, whereas other studies have reported reliable measures of lexical interactions shortly after learning (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Armstrong et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Batterink & Neville, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Coutanche & Thompson-Schill, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Borovsky et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kapnoula & McMurray, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, the interpretation of these behavioral effects as evidence of lexical-semantic integration is not straightforward.
One possibility is that recently established episodic associations contribute to the observed effects.
For instance, Korochkina et al. (2021) demonstrated that novel word distractors can produce significant semantic interference in a picture-word interference task 24 hours after learning.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr">Korochkina et al. (2021)</ref> demonstrated that novel word distractors can produce significant semantic interference in a picture-word interference task 24 hours after learning.

text.text: However, they argued that this effect is strongly modulated by the learning context and may arise from coactivation within episodic memory due to shared encoding details, rather than differences in the extent of their lexical-semantic integration.
In addition to episodic associations, strategic processes may contribute to behavioral evidence of semantic interactions for newly learned words.

Unlike automatic semantic activation, which is thought to rely more strongly on established lexical-semantic representations, strategic processing involves the use of task-related expectations or deliberate retrieval of semantic information (Neely, 1977) and may operate on recently acquired, non-integrated representations. Ball et al. (2025), for example, showed that behavioral priming for novel words can be influenced by strategic priming mechanisms.
text.formatted: Unlike automatic semantic activation, which is thought to rely more strongly on established lexical-semantic representations, strategic processing involves the use of task-related expectations or deliberate retrieval of semantic information <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Neely, 1977)</ref> and may operate on recently acquired, non-integrated representations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Ball et al. (2025)</ref>, for example, showed that behavioral priming for novel words can be influenced by strategic priming mechanisms.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that early behavioral evidence of lexical interactions does not necessarily imply lexical-semantic integration as similar effects may also arise from episodic and/or strategic processes.
Electrophysiological measures provide a complementary approach to this question.

The N400 is a centro-parietal negative-going ERP component peaking approximately 300-500 ms after stimulus onset and is sensitive to semantic expectancy, relatedness, lexicality, and contextual predictability (Kutas & Hillyard, 1980; Kutas & Federmeier, 2011).
text.formatted: The N400 is a centro-parietal negative-going ERP component peaking approximately 300-500 ms after stimulus onset and is sensitive to semantic expectancy, relatedness, lexicality, and contextual predictability <ref type="bibr">(Kutas & Hillyard, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The emergence of an N400 semantic relatedness effect, characterized by reduced N400 negativity for semantically related compared to unrelated word pairs, has been interpreted as evidence that newly learned words can engage in semantic processing, suggesting that newly learned words are beginning to be processed in ways resembling familiar words (Perfetti et al., 2005; Mestres-Missé et al., 2007; Bakker et al., 2015).

text.text: In previous work, our group examined lexical integration in the first language (L1) (Kaczer et al., 2018).

text.text: Using a semantic relatedness judgment task, participants judged whether a target word was semantically related or unrelated to a preceding prime.
Immediately after learning, newly learned words did not show a reliable N400 priming effect.

However, after a 48-hour delay, related targets elicited a reduced N400 compared with unrelated targets, accompanied by a behavioral semantic priming effect, with slower and more accurate responses to unrelated than related prime-target pairs.
This pattern suggests that the N400 can provide a neural measure of changes in semantic processing that emerge following learning.

Recent computational accounts conceptualize the N400 as indexing changes in an implicit probabilistic representation of meaning-corresponding to semantic prediction error (Rabovsky et al., 2018)-thereby linking it to predictive mechanisms within the semantic system.

text.text: Importantly, behavioral and N400 effects do not necessarily emerge in parallel. Korochkina et al. (2024), using a continuous primed lexical decision task designed to minimize strategic processing, found a small but reliable behavioral priming effect (7 ms) for novel L1 words after a 24-hour interval, but no corresponding N400 priming effect.

(2024)</ref>, using a continuous primed lexical decision task designed to minimize strategic processing, found a small but reliable behavioral priming effect (7 ms) for novel L1 words after a 24-hour interval, but no corresponding N400 priming effect.

text.text: Instead, novel words elicited late ERP modulations (500-800 ms), consistent with the Late Positive Complex (LPC), which has been associated with episodic retrieval, recollection, and controlled aspects of semantic processing (e.g., Juottonen et al., 1996; DeLong et al., 2014; Rugg & Curran, 2007).

text.text: Thus, later ERP activity may provide complementary information about the processes involved in recognizing and retrieving newly learned lexical representations.

Despite this growing literature, most studies of lexical learning have relied on highly controlled laboratory paradigms involving artificial learning, limited exposure, and relatively small sets of novel words.
This leaves open the question of how newly acquired vocabulary develops under more naturalistic conditions, where learning unfolds gradually through repeated and distributed practice.

This issue is particularly relevant for L2 learning, which differs from L1 word learning because new lexical forms are typically mapped onto concepts that are already represented in the learner's native language.
Mobile-assisted language learning provides an opportunity to investigate these processes in a more ecologically valid context.

For instance, a recent study by Leung et al. (2025) showed that short-term training of a non-native language using language-immersion apps elicited larger brain responses in preschool children compared to training using traditional flash cards.
text.formatted: For instance, a recent study by <ref type="bibr">Leung et al. (2025)</ref> showed that short-term training of a non-native language using language-immersion apps elicited larger brain responses in preschool children compared to training using traditional flash cards.

text.text: Among mobile-assisted learning platforms, Duolingo is one of the most widely used, offering structured, gamified learning experiences across multiple languages (Shortt et al., 2023; Cho & Castañeda, 2019).
text.formatted: Among mobile-assisted learning platforms, Duolingo is one of the most widely used, offering structured, gamified learning experiences across multiple languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Shortt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cho & Castañeda, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Numerous studies have reported that such tools improve lexical, grammatical, and oral language skills (Loewen et al., 2020; Kessler et al., 2025; Li & Bonk, 2025), although others have pointed out pedagogical limitations such as repetitive exercises, limited feedback, and shallow processing (e.g., García Botero et al., 2019; Rosell-Aguilar, 2017).

text.text: These environments differ from laboratory paradigms in several key respects: learning is distributed over a longer time, exposure is multimodal, and practice is often self-guided.

ERP studies in such contexts suggest that neural markers of lexical processing, including N400 modulations, can emerge relatively early and strengthen with continued exposure (e.g., McLaughlin et al., 2004; Stein et al., 2006; Soskey et al., 2016).
text.formatted: ERP studies in such contexts suggest that neural markers of lexical processing, including N400 modulations, can emerge relatively early and strengthen with continued exposure (e.g., <ref type="bibr">McLaughlin et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stein et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Soskey et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A further limitation of L2 research is its predominant focus on widely spoken languages such as English, often at the expense of underrepresented languages (Tommerdahl et al., 2024; García Botero et al., 2019).
text.formatted: A further limitation of L2 research is its predominant focus on widely spoken languages such as English, often at the expense of underrepresented languages <ref type="bibr">(Tommerdahl et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">García Botero et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Examining languages beyond English is theoretically informative because it allows researchers to test whether mechanisms identified in English-based paradigms generalize across different linguistic systems.

This is particularly relevant when word learning is examined in a naturalistic context, where the interaction between a typologically distinct L2 and an established L1 can be studied without reducing the learning process to highly controlled laboratory materials.

One such language is Guarani, an Indigenous South American language of the Tupi-Guarani family, spoken by approximately 6.5 million people across Paraguay, Argentina, Bolivia, and Brazil (Hornberger, 2006; Symeonidis, 2018; Rubin, 1968).
text.formatted: One such language is Guarani, an Indigenous South American language of the Tupi-Guarani family, spoken by approximately 6.5 million people across Paraguay, Argentina, Bolivia, and Brazil <ref type="bibr">(Hornberger, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Symeonidis, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Rubin, 1968)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its sociolinguistic prominence-it is one of the most widely spoken Indigenous languages of the Americas and an official language of Paraguay-Guarani remains largely overlooked in psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic research (but see Lucas et al., 2024; Mihalcea et al., 2025, for recent computational advances).
text.formatted: Despite its sociolinguistic prominence-it is one of the most widely spoken Indigenous languages of the Americas and an official language of Paraguay-Guarani remains largely overlooked in psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic research (but see <ref type="bibr">Lucas et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mihalcea et al., 2025, for recent computational advances)</ref>.

text.text: Guarani is genetically unrelated to Spanish, the native language of the participants in the present study, and shares few lexical items with it, apart from a limited number of borrowings.
It also differs substantially from Spanish in phonological, morphological, and grammatical structure.
For example, whereas Spanish exhibits grammatical gender and variable lexical stress, Guarani lacks gender marking and typically displays fixed word-level stress (Estigarribia, 2020).
Morphologically, it is agglutinative and mildly polysynthetic, with extensive affixation that allows multiple grammatical features to be encoded within single word forms.
These characteristics make Guarani a well-suited language for testing whether findings from L2 word-learning research generalize beyond the linguistic properties of Spanish and English.

At the same time, the naturalistic learning environment provided by Duolingo allows this question to be examined using real Guarani words rather than highly controlled laboratory materials, providing a more ecologically valid test of how newly learned words are processed.
The present study examined lexical-semantic processing following naturalistic L2 vocabulary learning through Duolingo.
Spanish native speakers learned Guarani vocabulary through the Duolingo platform over approximately five weeks, and we captured multiple learning metrics using Duolingo for Schools.

After reaching a predefined threshold of learning progress, participants attended a laboratory session, where they completed a semantic relatedness judgment task while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded.
This paradigm enabled us to assess lexical-semantic processing through modulation of the N400 and LPC components.
We compared words tested within 10 days of their most recent exposure (Recent condition) with words last practiced approximately 20 days earlier (Remote condition).

This manipulation allowed us to examine whether the level of exposure and the time elapsed since last practice modulates behavioral and neural indices of lexical-semantic processing in a naturalistic L2 learning context.
In addition, we examined whether aggregate measures of engagement from the learning platform were associated with behavioral and neural markers of learning.
>Materials and Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Materials and Methods</head>

text.text: The study consisted of two phases: an app-based language learning phase followed by a laboratory EEG experiment.
During the learning phase, the participants enrolled in a Duolingo Guarani course.
They were instructed to complete all the assigned lessons, from Section 1, Unit 1 to Section 3, Unit 4 of the Duolingo course (see 2.3.
Training phase: App-based Learning).
Their enrollment, progress and performance were monitored using Duolingo for Schools.
Upon completing the required vocabulary, they were invited to participate in a laboratory-based EEG experiment.
The training regime was designed to approximate naturalistic language learning conditions, prioritizing ecological validity over the level of exposure control typical of laboratory-based studies.

Participants were native speakers of Rioplatense Spanish, a variety spoken mainly in Argentina and Uruguay and characterized by features such as voseo (the use of vos as the second-person singular pronoun) and yeísmo rehilado (the postalveolar fricative realization of /ʝ/ and /ʎ/) (Coloma, 2018; Lipski, 2012; Resnick, 2012).
text.formatted: Participants were native speakers of Rioplatense Spanish, a variety spoken mainly in Argentina and Uruguay and characterized by features such as voseo (the use of vos as the second-person singular pronoun) and yeísmo rehilado (the postalveolar fricative realization of /ʝ/ and /ʎ/) <ref type="bibr">(Coloma, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lipski, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Resnick, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were 18-35 years old, had no prior knowledge of Guarani (apart from common loanwords in Rioplatense Spanish, such as "chipa" or "tereré", which were not used in the study), and were either undergraduate students or university graduates.
An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2007) to estimate the minimum sample size required for an analysis with within-subjects factors.

text.text: Using α = .05, desired power of 1 -β = .95, and an effect size estimate of f = 0.3, derived from a conservative approach of prior ERP research (Liu & van Hell, 2020), the analysis indicated a minimum sample size of N ≥ 20.

text.text: A total of 96 individuals completed the recruitment form and began learning Guarani through the Duolingo platform.
Twenty-four participants (19-35 years; M = 24.75, SD = 4.17; 15 female) completed the required learning assignments and participated in the EEG session.
Participants who withdrew during the study reported lack of time or waning interest.
No participants were excluded due to insufficient learning performance, as all participants who completed the learning phase achieved the predefined learning criteria.

Data from three participants were subsequently excluded from the EEG analyses because of excessive trial rejection or a high proportion of noisy or unusable channels during preprocessing, resulting in a final EEG sample of 21 participants.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Instituto de Investigaciones Médicas Alfredo Lanari.
All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Participants studied Guarani autonomously using Duolingo for an average of 36.6 days (SD = 13.2), during which they acquired basic vocabulary, including words related to people, animals, and food.
The course followed a strictly linear and thematic progression, with lessons and units arranged in a predetermined order.

The standard sequence of lessons provided by Duolingo was not modified for the purposes of this study: participants completed the lessons in the same order and format as regular learners using the platform.
Participants completed 69 lessons, each consisting of 15 tasks.
These were organized into three thematic sections, and each section was divided into subsections.
Lessons lasted on average 2.85 minutes (median: 2 min, IQR: 1 min).
The majority of tasks consisted of word-bank exercises, in which participants arranged given words in L1 or L2 to translate a sentence in the other language.
A smaller proportion of tasks required uncued written production, in which participants typed responses without provided options.
Words and sentences in Guarani (L2) were presented visually with optional auditory input that could be enabled or disabled by the user.
Grammar and vocabulary were thus acquired through repeated translation practice and feedback on errors.
Examples of these tasks are shown in Figure 1B.
text.formatted: Examples of these tasks are shown in Figure <ref type="figure">1B</ref>.

text.text: New vocabulary could be introduced or previously learned material reviewed, and incorrectly answered tasks had to be repeated until a correct response was provided.

All participants were exposed to the same set of 155 Guarani (L2) words-including pronouns, nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, conjunctions and interjections-as the course followed a fixed progression.

Due to the adaptive nature of the platform, the exact number of exposures per word varied across participants, although items were typically encountered multiple times across lessons through both initial presentation and subsequent review.
Participants' progress was monitored using Duolingo for Schools, an online platform designed for classroom management and learner tracking.
A virtual classroom was created to enrol participants and systematically observe their activity.
The platform allowed the assignment of specific lessons and provided detailed records of daily progress, performance metrics, and engagement with optional content.

text.text: All stimuli were presented in prime-target pairs.
Target words.
A total of 120 words were selected: 40 in Spanish (L1) and 80 in Guarani (L2).
The characteristics of the selected stimuli are detailed below.
Guarani (L2) words were drawn from the first three sections of the Duolingo Guarani course to ensure that all participants had encountered and learned them prior to the EEG session.
This constraint, however, limited flexibility in word selection, resulting in a broader range of word lengths (1-13 letters) and grammatical categories.
The 80 Guarani words were divided into two conditions differing in learning recency: L2 Remote and L2 Recent.
The L2 Remote condition comprised words (n = 39) learned during the first two sections of the course-typically within the initial 26 days of training.
In contrast, the L2 Recent condition included words (n = 41) introduced in the third section, generally encountered during the final 10 days.
Thus, the L2 Remote-L2 Recent distinction is intended to capture graded differences in lexical integration.
On average, L2 Remote words were learned and practiced during approximately 26.4 days (SD = 9.0), whereas L2 Recent words were learned and practiced during approximately 10.2 days (SD = 5.9).
The amount of practice of L2 Remote words during the learning of L2 Recent words was not substantial.
Particularly, practice of L2 Remote words was consigned to one subsection during Section 3 (3-2).
Only some pronouns (me, you) and basic verbs (to eat / to drink) were practised during the rest of Section 3 in order to form logical and grammatical sentences.
The average learning and practice timeline is shown in Figure 1A.

text.text: Spanish (L1) words (n = 40) were drawn from the EsPal-Spanish Lexical Database (Duchon et al., 2013), and selected based on a minimum frequency of 0.25 per million words in the EsPal corpus (range: 0.26 -726.61).

text.text: All Spanish words were nouns and ranged from 3 to 9 letters in length.
Spanish items were selected for semantic compatibility with the Guarani targets.
Given that the learnt Guarani words refer to basic concepts, relatively high-frequency Spanish counterparts were to be expected.
Primes.

Each target word was paired with two Spanish (L1) prime words, yielding 240 word pairs: one prime was semantically related to the target word (Related condition), and the other was unrelated (Unrelated condition).
Primes were selected from the EsPal corpus, with frequencies ranging from 0.04 to 2,290 per million words, and lengths ranging from 2 to 10 letters.
Most primes were nouns (205 out of 240), though some varied in part of speech to align with the variability in the Guarani target words.
Importantly, the primes were not the direct translation of the target words.
These L1 primes were chosen to ensure comparable distributional properties across languages and conditions.
To prevent participants from adopting any specific semantic strategy, both taxonomic and thematic relations were included in the 3 conditions, and their strength was varied across pairs.
Importantly, all word-pair distributions were then assessed using a FastText word-embedding model (Mikolov et al., 2017) to compute cosine similarity.

text.text: A practice block consisting of 10 prime-target pairs with feedback was followed by four experimental blocks of 60 pairs each.
The order of the pairs within each block was randomized for every participant.
The experimental pairs included 39 Remote words and 41 Recent words, each presented with one semantically related prime and one unrelated prime.
A trial began with a 250-ms blank screen followed by a 500-ms fixation cross (Fig.
The prime was then displayed for 500 ms, followed by a 250-ms blank interval and the target word, which appeared for 1000 ms.
This design implied a constant 750 ms stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA).
Next, a semantic decision prompt ("¿Están relacionados?"
[Are they related?]) remained on the screen for 2000 ms, during which participants indicated whether the two words were semantically related by pressing a key ("YES": right arrow; "NO": left arrow).
If no response was made within 2000 ms, the next trial commenced automatically.
Participants were allowed to respond as soon as the target word appeared, and no feedback was provided. answer during the last two screens (in red).
For each dependent variable we began with the maximal random-effects structure justified by the design, including by-participant and by-item random slopes for the fixed effects and their interaction.
Random-effects terms that were not supported by the data (variance components estimated at or near zero, or correlations at or near ±1 in the variance-covariance matrix) were candidates for removal.
Each candidate was removed one at a time, starting with the term with the smallest variance, and the reduced model was compared with the model including that term.
The reduced model was retained whenever its AIC was equal to or lower than that of the more complex model; otherwise, the term was kept.
This procedure was repeated until no further term met the criteria for removal.
Specifications of each final model are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

Accuracy was defined at the trial level as a binary variable indicating whether the response was correct (1) or incorrect (0), and was analysed over all trials with a generalized linear mixed-effects model (binomial family, logit link) fitted with lme4 (Bates et al., 2015).

text.text: This study investigated whether vocabulary learned in an ecologically valid, app-based environment could engage the semantic system of adult second-language (L2) learners and whether the expression of such processing changed as a function of learning recency.

By combining a naturalistic Guarani learning experience using Duolingo with a laboratory-based semantic relatedness judgement task and EEG measurements, we examined behavioral and electrophysiological indices of the processing of recently and more remotely learned L2 words.

At the behavioral level, RTs show that participants responded faster to semantically related than unrelated targets, indicating that their responses were sensitive to the semantic relationship between the newly acquired L2 words with the familiar L1 words.
Accuracy results also showed an effect of semantic relatedness, with participants responding more accurately to Unrelated than Related pairs.

This pattern is compatible with the demands of the semantic relatedness judgement task, in which identifying that two words are related may require evaluating the strength or nature of their semantic relationship, whereas unrelated pairs may provide a less ambiguous basis for the decision (Kaczer et al., 2018 Khanzhyn et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This pattern is compatible with the demands of the semantic relatedness judgement task, in which identifying that two words are related may require evaluating the strength or nature of their semantic relationship, whereas unrelated pairs may provide a less ambiguous basis for the decision <ref type="bibr">(Kaczer et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr">Khanzhyn et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The electrophysiological findings provide complementary evidence.
A semantic relatedness effect was observed in the N400 time window at Cz, with more negative amplitudes for Unrelated than Related targets.

As the N400 is sensitive to the ease with which words are accessed and processed in semantic context (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011), the present effect becomes compatible with the involvement of semantic processing during the access to newly learned L2 words.
text.formatted: As the N400 is sensitive to the ease with which words are accessed and processed in semantic context <ref type="bibr">(Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)</ref>, the present effect becomes compatible with the involvement of semantic processing during the access to newly learned L2 words.

text.text: In addition, the LPC shows a semantic relatedness effect at Pz.

Importantly, while these results indicate that the newly learned L2 words were accessible and could support semantic judgements and modulate the N400 amplitude, this effect should not be interpreted straightforwardly as evidence of automatic semantic activation.

Because the task explicitly requires participants to evaluate the relationship between the prime and target, and given the relatively long SOA, performance may involve controlled processing, episodic retrieval, expectancy, or task-related strategies in addition to automatic spreading activation within semantic representations (Korochkina et al., 2024; Ball et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Because the task explicitly requires participants to evaluate the relationship between the prime and target, and given the relatively long SOA, performance may involve controlled processing, episodic retrieval, expectancy, or task-related strategies in addition to automatic spreading activation within semantic representations <ref type="bibr">(Korochkina et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Ball et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Learning recency (i.e., the comparison between Recent and Remote L2 words) did not produce an overall difference in accuracy, response times, or mean N400 amplitude.
Importantly, however, recency modulated some of the effects of semantic relatedness.
At the behavioral level, the difference in accuracy between Unrelated and Related pairs was smaller for Remote than for Recent words.
This interaction suggests that learning history influenced performance when participants evaluated semantic relationships between newly acquired words and familiar targets.
At the electrophysiological level, the N400 Relatedness effect at Pz was larger for L2 Remote than for L2 Recent words.
Thus, the Relatedness effects differed in direction across behavioral accuracy and N400 amplitude.
Nevertheless, these findings may reflect complementary aspects of semantic processing.
In accuracy, a smaller difference between Related and Unrelated pairs may indicate reduced difficulty in identifying semantic relationships.
In contrast, a larger N400 Relatedness effect may reflect greater sensitivity to semantic relationships.
Both patterns are therefore compatible with facilitated semantic processing for Remote words, although they do not necessarily indicate a greater degree of lexical-semantic integration.

This finding is broadly in line with our previous work (Kaczer et al., 2018), in which newly learned words did not reliably elicit N400 semantic priming shortly after learning, whereas this effect emerged after 48 h.
text.formatted: This finding is broadly in line with our previous work <ref type="bibr">(Kaczer et al., 2018)</ref>, in which newly learned words did not reliably elicit N400 semantic priming shortly after learning, whereas this effect emerged after 48 h.

text.text: The present results extend this finding to vocabulary acquired through a naturalistic L2 learning environment, suggesting that learning recency can also modulate the neural markers of semantic relatedness effects.
However, this interpretation should be considered cautiously, as the critical interaction emerged at Pz but not at Cz.
Given the typically broad centro-parietal distribution of the N400 (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011), we had expected the interaction to emerge at both electrodes.
text.formatted: Given the typically broad centro-parietal distribution of the N400 <ref type="bibr">(Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)</ref>, we had expected the interaction to emerge at both electrodes.

text.text: The comparison between L1 and L2 items provides an additional perspective on the findings.
At the behavioral level, participants were more accurate and responded faster to L1 than to L2 targets.

These differences are consistent with the greater familiarity and more extensive experience participants had with L1 vocabulary and provide a broad behavioral indication that L2 processing remained distinct from that of established lexical representations.
The electrophysiological findings showed a similar distinction between L1 and L2 processing.

L1 targets elicited more negative N400 amplitudes than L2 targets, a pattern that differs from findings in which less integrated or newly learned items have been associated with larger N400 amplitudes (Borovsky et al., 2010; Friedrich & Friederici, 2008).
text.formatted: L1 targets elicited more negative N400 amplitudes than L2 targets, a pattern that differs from findings in which less integrated or newly learned items have been associated with larger N400 amplitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Borovsky et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Friedrich & Friederici, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: However, similar L1-L2 patterns have been reported in studies of L2 learning conducted in more ecological contexts (Soskey et al., 2016).
text.formatted: However, similar L1-L2 patterns have been reported in studies of L2 learning conducted in more ecological contexts <ref type="bibr">(Soskey et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the L1-L2 difference in N400 amplitude should not be interpreted straightforwardly as evidence for greater or lesser lexical-semantic integration.

L1 targets also elicited more positive LPC amplitudes than L2 targets at both Cz and Pz, further indicating differences between established L1 and newly acquired L2 words in later stages of processing, similar to the reports of Bakker et al. (2015).
text.formatted: L1 targets also elicited more positive LPC amplitudes than L2 targets at both Cz and Pz, further indicating differences between established L1 and newly acquired L2 words in later stages of processing, similar to the reports of <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bakker et al. (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike the N400, however, the LPC did not show a reliable modulation by learning recency, suggesting that the effects of learning recency were not consistently expressed across later processing stages.
One possible explanation for the L1-L2 difference is that it emerges from cross-language processing dynamics rather than differences in integration per se.
In the present design, L1 targets were preceded by L1 primes, whereas L2 targets followed L1 primes, creating a cross-language context for the L2 condition.

Prior work suggests that cross-language semantic processing can modulate N400 amplitude, potentially reflecting differences in the automaticity of semantic activation and the contribution of controlled processing (Martin et al., 2009; Midgley et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Prior work suggests that cross-language semantic processing can modulate N400 amplitude, potentially reflecting differences in the automaticity of semantic activation and the contribution of controlled processing <ref type="bibr">(Martin et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Midgley et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Participants may also have engaged different processing strategies for L2 targets, such as allocating greater attentional resources or managing potential L1 interference, which could modulate N400 amplitude independently of integration strength.

Another possibility is that the reduced N400 amplitude for L2 items reflects a greater contribution of episodic memory processes relative to the more automatic semantic processing associated with well-established lexical representations, as proposed in recent work on newly learned L1 words (e.g., Korochkina et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Another possibility is that the reduced N400 amplitude for L2 items reflects a greater contribution of episodic memory processes relative to the more automatic semantic processing associated with well-established lexical representations, as proposed in recent work on newly learned L1 words (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Korochkina et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Regardless of the precise mechanism, the L1-L2 differences across behavioral and electrophysiological measures underscore that newly acquired L2 words continued to be processed differently from established L1 words.

At the same time, the direction of the N400 difference highlights the importance of considering language context and task demands when interpreting absolute N400 amplitude in studies of newly acquired L2 vocabulary.

Turning to the comparison across the three Word Type conditions (L1, L2 Remote, and L2 Recent), we initially expected that L2 Remote words, having been learned earlier and experienced over a longer period, would show a processing profile more similar to that of familiar L1 words.
However, the present findings do not provide clear evidence of such convergence.
Although accuracy for Related pairs was descriptively closer to L1 for L2 Remote than for L2 Recent items, the electrophysiological results showed a different pattern.

In particular, the N400 relatedness effect appeared larger for L2 Remote than for L1 items at Cz, and differences in the LPC responses were also apparent between these conditions at the same electrode.
These observations suggest that differences in learning history did not result in a uniformly more L1-like processing profile.

However, similarity to L1 should not be considered a direct measure of lexical-semantic integration, as electrophysiological responses may differ across languages due to linguistic properties, familiarity, and the contribution of strategic processes.

Previous longitudinal research has also shown that N400 responses to L2 words change progressively with learning experience without necessarily becoming identical to those elicited by L1 words (Soskey et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Previous longitudinal research has also shown that N400 responses to L2 words change progressively with learning experience without necessarily becoming identical to those elicited by L1 words <ref type="bibr">(Soskey et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: An important consideration when interpreting the learning-recency effects is that the L2 Remote and L2 Recent conditions differed not only in elapsed time since learning but also in their exposure histories.
Remote words had been encountered over a longer period and therefore accumulated a different amount and distribution of practice than Recent words.
Consequently, the stronger N400 Relatedness effect observed for Remote words cannot be attributed to elapsed consolidation time alone.
It may reflect the combined influence of time since learning, cumulative exposure, distributed practice, or other characteristics of the participants' learning history.
This limitation is closely tied to the naturalistic nature of the learning environment.

Unlike experimenter-controlled training paradigms, participants acquired Guarani vocabulary through the standard Duolingo course over several weeks, with repeated exposure distributed across their ongoing learning experience.
This approach allowed us to examine the neurocognitive consequences of vocabulary acquired under conditions that more closely resemble real-world L2 learning.

At the same time, the app's built-in review system provided continued exposure to previously learned vocabulary, potentially reducing differences between the Remote and Recent sets by the time of testing.
The aggregate learning measures available from the app provide a similar constraint.
XP, total learning time, and active days offer a general description of participants' engagement with the course, but do not capture the item-level history of individual words.

The absence of significant associations between these measures and behavioral or electrophysiological outcomes should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the amount of practice was unrelated to the observed effects.
Rather, these aggregate measures may not have been sufficiently sensitive to the specific characteristics of individual-word learning that shaped performance at the time of testing.
The over-reliance on English across the cognitive sciences has been argued to limit the generality of their conclusions (Blasi et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The over-reliance on English across the cognitive sciences has been argued to limit the generality of their conclusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Blasi et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The present study contributes to broadening the linguistic scope of this research by examining the acquisition of Guarani, an Indigenous language of South America that remains underrepresented in cognitive neuroscience.

Importantly, Guarani differs substantially from Spanish in its morphological structure, phonology, and orthographic conventions, with relatively limited lexical overlap between the two languages (Estigarribia, 2020).

These differences may pose additional challenges for L2 vocabulary learning, as learners cannot readily rely on similarities with familiar L1 word forms (Ellis & Beaton, 1993; De Groot & Keijzer, 2000).
text.formatted: These differences may pose additional challenges for L2 vocabulary learning, as learners cannot readily rely on similarities with familiar L1 word forms <ref type="bibr">(Ellis & Beaton, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr">De Groot & Keijzer, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond its linguistic characteristics, Guarani also has sociolinguistic relevance, given its longstanding presence in Argentina and neighboring Paraguay, and its history of stigmatization and unequal social prestige relative to Spanish in certain contexts (Medina et al., 2020; Zajícová, 2009).
text.formatted: Beyond its linguistic characteristics, Guarani also has sociolinguistic relevance, given its longstanding presence in Argentina and neighboring Paraguay, and its history of stigmatization and unequal social prestige relative to Spanish in certain contexts <ref type="bibr">(Medina et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zajícová, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Including Guarani in neurocognitive research therefore contributes to increasing the scientific visibility of a language that remains underrepresented despite its regional and cultural significance.

More broadly, this highlights the importance of expanding language learning research beyond socially dominant languages to include those that, despite their widespread use and cultural significance, have historically received less social and scientific recognition.
Below, we briefly discuss some methodological considerations and how they might be addressed in future work.

Regarding our electrophysiological findings, it is important to consider that the present study used a 30-channel EEG montage, providing relatively coarse spatial sampling compared with denser recording systems.
In this sense, the different patterns observed at Cz and Pz should be interpreted cautiously.

Although Cz and Pz are commonly examined in relation to the N400, the present montage does not allow us to determine whether differences between these locations reflect genuinely distinct neural patterns or variability in the spatial distribution of the component.
The modest EEG sample and the number of trials available for each condition limit the sensitivity of the study to detect smaller effects, particularly interactions.
Accordingly, null findings should not be taken as evidence that learning recency has no influence on L2 lexical processing.

Future studies combining larger samples with denser EEG recordings and more controlled manipulation of exposure and elapsed time will be important for testing the robustness and spatial specificity of the present findings.

More broadly, the difficulty of disentangling recency, cumulative exposure, and the temporal distribution of practice reflects a fundamental characteristic of naturalistic language learning: these factors are intertwined throughout the learning process.
Although controlled experimental paradigms are essential for isolating specific mechanisms, their findings may not fully capture the complexity of real-world L2 acquisition.

Conversely, naturalistic approaches provide an opportunity to examine how different aspects of learning history jointly relate to language processing, even when their individual contributions cannot be established.
This highlights the complementary value of controlled and naturalistic approaches.
An additional limitation concerns the explicit nature of the semantic relatedness task.

Because participants were required to judge whether word pairs were semantically related, the observed effects may involve controlled retrieval and strategic processing, making it difficult to establish the extent to which they reflect automatic semantic activation.
Future studies using paradigms with reduced strategic demands, such as implicit semantic priming tasks (Tamminen & Gaskell, 2013), could help address this distinction.
text.formatted: Future studies using paradigms with reduced strategic demands, such as implicit semantic priming tasks <ref type="bibr">(Tamminen & Gaskell, 2013)</ref>, could help address this distinction.

text.text: Longitudinal designs, combined with more systematic measures of proficiency and exposure, could further clarify how behavioral and electrophysiological markers change with learning experience.

Together, these approaches could help determine whether semantic relatedness effects in newly learned L2 words reflect emerging lexical-semantic integration or processing supported by episodic and strategic mechanisms.
This study shows that vocabulary acquired through naturalistic, app-based L2 learning can engage semantic processing during a controlled semantic relatedness task.

Importantly, differences between recently and remotely learned words suggest that lexical-semantic processing may vary as a function of learning history, including the recency, amount, and temporal distribution of exposure.

More broadly, these findings highlight the value of combining ecologically valid language-learning environments with electrophysiological measures to investigate the neurocognitive consequences of L2 vocabulary learning, and of extending this research to underrepresented languages such as Guarani.

Behavioral results, based on the sample of 24 participants, are illustrated in Figure 3.

OverviewWe examined whether the new L2 items showed evidence of lexical-semantic integration by testing their sensitivity to semantic relatedness with L1 primes.
A semantic relatedness task (adapted fromBakker et al., 2015) was performed.
text.formatted: A semantic relatedness task (adapted from<ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bakker et al., 2015)</ref> was performed.

text.text: The present experiment was conducted following a passive reading task, not described here(Igarreta et al., in preparation).
Figure 2.
Trial example of the semantic decision experiment.
Participants could recorded from 30 electrodes placed according to the international 10/10 system (Electro-Cap International Inc.) using the Akonic Bio PC system.
Data were recorded online with reference to the left mastoid and re-referenced offline to the average of the left and right mastoids.
Electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ.
The recording system applied a hardware notch filter at 50 Hz, a 1st-order high-pass filter at 0.5 Hz, and a low-pass filter at 100 Hz.
EEG signals were sampled at 256 Hz.
An additional 8th-order high-pass filter at 0.1 Hz was applied offline.
Because the hardware cutoff is higher, the effective high-pass characteristic of the analysed data is determined by the 0.5 Hz filter.
ERPs were time-locked to the onset of the target word.
Epoch length was 800 ms, plus a 200 ms pre-stimulus interval as baseline.
EEG signal processing and ERP analysis were carried out with the Python MNE library(Gramfort et al., 2014).
Ocular artefacts were removed using Independent Component Analysis (ICA)-based correction, with components associated with eye activity identified primarily from Fp1, Fp2, F7, and F8 channels.
Automatic rejection was used to exclude all epochs containing artefacts using the AutoReject function from the Python AutoReject library(Jas et al., 2017).
Behavioral and electrophysiological data were analysed with the same modelling strategy, implemented in R (version 4.4.0).
All analyses used (generalized) linear mixed-effects models with fixed effects of Word Type (L1, L2 Recent, L2 Remote), Relatedness (Related, Unrelated), and their interaction.
Fixed effects were parameterized using centred and orthogonal contrasts(Schad et al., 2020): Word Type was coded with two contrasts, L1 vs.
text.formatted: Fixed effects were parameterized using centred and orthogonal contrasts<ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Schad et al., 2020)</ref>: Word Type was coded with two contrasts, L1 vs.

text.text: L2 (collapsing L2 Recent and L2 Remote) and L2 Remote vs.
L2 Recent (hereafter, recency); Relatedness was coded as Unrelated vs.
Related.
Each model coefficient thus corresponds to one planned contrast, so that our hypotheses are tested directly on the coefficients without post hoc comparisons.
Two interaction terms follow from this coding.
The L1 vs.
L2 × Relatedness interaction tests whether the relatedness effect differs between newly learned L2 words and familiar L1 words.
The Recency × Relatedness interaction, which is of particular interest, tests whether the relatedness effect varies as a function of the time elapsed since learning.
